projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Martin Kujala was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War Two veteran Marvin John Kujala. Mr. Kujala served in the US Marine Corps with the 15th Marines and with Headquarters Company of the 29th Marines. Martin's highest rank was corporal and he served in the Pacific Theater. I'm Tom Swope and this recording was made at Mr. Kujala's home in Painesville, Ohio on September 17, 2002. Martin was 75 at the time of this recording. Where were you living when America entered World War Two?

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: In Fairport. Well, no. I was living in Hamden. My father died in September of '41 and my mother and I were on a farm and we just couldn't--I was only 14 years old. So I couldn't handle--her and I couldn't handle the dairy herd that we had. So my oldest brother moved in and then my mother and I moved to Fairport. And I was living in Fairport. Yeah, I was living in Fairport Harbor. No, no. We were still in Hamden. We were still in Hamden, yeah, when December 7th happened. And we happened to be visiting some friends on North St. Clair Street in Painesville and I had been in the house and I heard it on the radio and was completely overwhelmed. So I entered the Marine Corps in January of '45. I was only 17 years old but I managed to get through. I went through boot camp at Perris Island. Then I believe it was about six weeks of boot camp and they decided to make--make me a radio operator. Why, I don't know because I didn't know diddly about radios and--but they put me--they put myself and some, I don't know, three or four other guys from the platoon into an old Quonset hut and we sat there and listened to code for about 16 hours a day, seven days a week. And at first I didn't think I'd ever learn it but when it was--finally when they--about after two weeks, why, they--I was beginning to get it. So as a result I was a--they made me a radio operator and I didn't even get a leave, my boot leave home. Went from Perris Island to--got on a train and ended up in front of the ship in Norfolk, Virginia. Got off the train and went right aboard ship and away we went. So we ended up in Guam and that's where the division was--was being formed, the Sixth Division. The only division that was formed overseas and disbanded oversees of the Marine Corps. So... But we were aboard ship when Iwo Jima was going on but we--they could have used us there I suppose if it--if they needed us but they--they saved us for Okinawa. And that happened Easter Sunday, April 1st of 1945, and I was in--I was assigned to the Sixth JASCO, Joint Assault Signal Company, and I went in probably about the, I don't know, fourth or fifth wave. Not much happened on the beach. There was some--some sniper fire and some occasional artillery rounds and so on but it was--it wasn't anything like Iwo Jima, for instance, when they hit the beach there. We--we just walked in almost unopposed and took very few casualties. So... But I was assigned to Item Battery, 15th Marines, an artillery outfit, and I was to be a forward observer and--but this happened after. I was still in Sixth JASCO and we just kind of--our--our part of it swung northward on Okinawa, which is the easier end of the island. And I don't remember now. It's been so many years I don't remember all these things anymore. But the northern end of the island was the easier operation. When the real trouble began was when they secured the northern end so to speak and started working southward from the, what, the Shuri--what do they call it? The Shuri Castle Line or something and that's when--that's when they really had had problems. And it was--it was a tough fight down there. I wasn't involved too much in that down there for whatever reason. They were--I got--I guess I lucked out. I just stayed behind when my outfit was headed southward and when April, May, June, toward the end of June the island was finally secured and they kept me on Okinawa because they were--they were figuring that Japan was going to be next. The--the--and that was going to be--we all worried about that because that was going to be a one tough fight if we had to hit the mainland of Japan. So they started shipping--once the island was secured they started shipping people toward China. I eventually went to China and landed in Sing Dao in what, October, September or October of '45. I was there in time to see the Japanese surrender at the racetrack in Sing Dao, China. And--and then we were all right until Mao Tse Tung started giving us all kinds of hassle and I finally got home in what? '46. I got discharged I think it was in October of '46. So that's--that's--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mao Tse Tung was giving you hassle in China?

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What exactly was happening there?

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: Yes. He just--he just wanted us out of--out of China. They--he was strictly Communist and he didn't want any part of us. In fact, it got to the point that if we went on liberty in town you had to go in groups because what was happening some guys would go by themselves and would be killed on the street. And so it was--they were starting to clamp down. You don't go by yourself. You go in groups if you're going to go into town. So--but that's--and then he was--whenever we went out on--take our line crews out, linemen and stuff like that, we always had to have escort and armed escort because they'd be out in the hills and they'd be sniping at us. But he was--he was pretty nasty to us. So--and I think it was 1948 they finally left China altogether. Because for whatever reason they didn't--they didn't stay there any--any longer than that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Would you describe your job as forward observer.

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: It was my job to get as close to enemy lines as you could and with a--with grids or sharp--with grids on it try to direct fire for my--for Item Battery and if there was anything that I saw that should be fired at. On occasion--one occasion why I even worked with the Navy. There was a cruiser and he had some pretty big stuff and I happened to get in touch with them and they sent a few rounds over. Now, those sound like boxcars going through there so--but that's--that's basically what it amounted to. Try to find a good place where you can observe and not be observed yourself and call in for--for fire.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were the cruisers pretty accurate when they fired?

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: Yeah, their accuracy was pretty good. The only thing was--was on occasions why, you'd get a short shot. Sometimes their powder bags weren't what they should be, you know. In fact, that happened to me. This one round was close enough that it picked me up and out of my foxhole and knocked me out for a while and, in fact, they--they found me and took me to an aid station. It had ruptured my eardrums so--but aside from that why, I didn't have--I guess I was lucky.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How long before you went back on the line after that?

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: I think I was back there for about a week and finally when my hearing was coming back and so--now when they--nurses look at my ears why, they--oh, you got all kinds of tracks in there. And I'm hard of hearing now but--and I think a lot of it is due to especially my right ear. So a lot of it's due to that so--but that's about it. That's it. So...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, I'm interested more when you said when you went in on Okinawa you were not under fire, correct?

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: Not much, no. There was some intermittent fire. It just wasn't--it was basically an unopposed landing. But then they started stiffening up after--after we were there and I don't remember the time table. I think--I think we--we reached Yontan Airfield the first day if I'm not mistaken and they figured that was going to take at least a week to get to that. But what--what they had done was they took and concentrated their troops on the southern end of the island and there they had the caves and these Okinawan cemeteries. They had like what do you--like a sentry box and they used to hide in them. And they were hard to--hard to get at. So--and they--they--the sentry boxes weren't hard. If you knew someone was there, why, you could knock them out. But what would happen they'd let us get through and then hit us in the back. And so we started watching those places pretty close. Tried to go around them when you could if you ran across them. So...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember the first time that you--you were under fire?

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: Yeah. It was--it was Yontan Airfield and I think the--it had been pretty well taken. And as I recall we were going across the airfield and they started dropping mortars and artillery rounds on us so--and we were in the open. We just--we just ran and we took some casualties there. I don't know how many but that was the first time under intense, intense fire. So...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What were you feeling when you knew they were actually shooting at you?

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: That's amazing. I think--I think I was so scared to death. You know, I don't know what I was feeling. I know I was scared. Just a 17-year-old kid and I turned 18 on the 3rd of April but anyhow it was fear. That was--that was the ultimate I think. I was scared to death and nights especially. Once we got there and night started coming on, nights were scary. I was--I was scared. I didn't sleep good. We tried to have two people to a foxhole, you know, so the one could sleep and the other one keep an eye open. But you're always thinking geez, don't let him fall asleep, too, you know. So--but that's what goes through your mind.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were there organized counterattacks by the Japanese or was it individual little things?

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: No. Not--not organized as such. They--they didn't--like the Banzai attacks from before other islands. By that time they had come to the realization that that was not too smart. They were losing too many troops because our fire power was so, so great. And organized attacks, no, not--oh, there might have been as we got farther north a couple of occasions we had some organized attacks but no great amount. No great amount. And we were able to thwart those all right with where I was. See, all I can speak of is in my own--my own type of--but now as they got--went south and it wasn't so much organized attacks as it was they were dug in--into these caves. And any--you know, any--what do I want to say? They were--they were so well concealed that it took--a lot of instances it took flame throwers. And if you'd get a tank close, a flame-throwing tank, those were beautiful to see if you could get them close enough because they can put a lot--a lot of flame into a hole. You'd throw grenades in. Somebody--if somebody was there with a BF--with a BAR they'd, you know, empty the magazine. And you hear that old cliche when in doubt empty the magazine. And that's what they did in some of those holes. So--and if you had--had the opportunity, why, in some instances, why, the caves were down where tanks with bulldozer blades on them could just fill them up. Just kind of what we felt was they were burying them alive but come to find out that these things stretched all over. You couldn't --if you closed one hole they had another one where they could go to or tunnels and that was--it was something else.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you encounter any civilians at Okinawa?

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: Yeah. On the south end of the island civilians were there and the Japanese had scared them to the point where they were so afraid of us that they were jumping off of cliffs. They did--they did the same thing on Saipan, too. But the Japanese had them so afraid of us that if the Marines get you you're--you're dead. They'll rape your women and kill your boys and men. And so they--they were jumping off cliffs but...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have any close buddies on Okinawa?

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: I had one close buddy and he--I lost him. He was a forward observer, too. And a guy by the name of Mickey Shaunessy from Brooklyn, New York. We were an odd couple. I don't know how we got together, but we went--we got--we went through boot camp together and we went to radio school together and we--we were together all the while. And about oh, three weeks, four weeks after we had been on Okinawa he was hit by a sniper. But we had made plans of when the war was over we were going to Alaska and Homestead and we had all kinds of plans. But he was--he was--he was a good buddy. And he had no family that I know of. I thought he told me he had a sister but I don't know how. I think I tried to reach a Shaunessy. Of course, there's probably a lot of Shaunessys in Brooklyn anyhow but I never--I never was able to make contact with anybody but he told me he was an orphan. So no parents that I know of but we--we hit it off pretty good and it was--it was rough for me when--when he died but he's buried there at Okinawa now so--but that's...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you able to do anything to relieve the tension when you were in Okinawa, entertainment or anything?

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: We--we had a USO tour come in. I don't even remember who they--who they were. There was talk that Bob Hope was supposed to come but it was--it was too--too hot. It was maybe a month after we had some--I can't think of the name of the outfit, but it was a USO tour but it was still--it was still pretty hectic because I think Okinawa lasted for what, close to 82 days? And just no--not much of that going on at that--afterwards, why, we had outfits coming in. But during the--during the battle, why, we were behind the lines quite a ways and just a small outfit. A couple of girls and they sang and danced I guess and that--that was it. So...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember anything about mail call? Any letters from home, that sort of thing?

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: Oh, yeah, yeah. You lived for that. You lived for that, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any special packages you remember getting?

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: Yeah. My sister sent me some chocolate chip cookies. They were kind of dried out by the time I got them but they still tasted awful, awful good.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you share them with the rest of the guys?

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yeah. You couldn't--you couldn't sit there by yourself and scarf them up. You shared them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, after the 82 days the island was declared secure. Were you still fighting guys after that 82 days, Japanese?

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: I guess I--they were--I heard of instances where they were--they were still conducting patrols, you know. And on occasion I guess they did shoot--shoot some that hadn't given up and--because they--we didn't take very many prisoners. Very few. I don't--I read somewhere but I don't remember what it was now how many prisoners they took. But they preferred to die rather than surrender. So--but that's...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Obviously it was just a couple of weeks into it when FDR died. Do you remember hearing that news?

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. That was--that was a shock. That was a shock to everybody. And we wondered what's going to happen now, you know, because he died in the middle of a war and--but, yeah, it shocked everybody. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: A lot of sadness among the guys?

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah, for the most part because he was the only president during the whole war, you know, and they looked for--to him for leadership and he was our president. So...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you were probably in China when the first atom bomb was dropped; is that right?

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: No, no. We were still on Okinawa and that's what we were pondering. We had secured the island and I think they dropped the bomb in August, was it not?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: Yeah. We heard that, and then the second bomb and then we heard about the surrender and--but that was--yeah, I was still on Okinawa. They--they kept me there for--I was working on radio stuff because they had figured they'd use Okinawa as quite a communications center for the attack on Japan. And some people had already left for--oh, after the war was over it was, I don't know, just a few days and they started shipping some people out. Some people were--were shipped home. They had enough points to because some--some--some of our troops were veterans of different island campaigns so they had picked up the points. And they were--they were gone quite--very quick really. So I didn't have enough points to get out of there that soon. So that's why they shipped me to China then finally.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you were there were you actually training for the invasion, going through any exercises to train?

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: No, not really. Not really because June--there was only about a month that we were cleaning up, you know, after securing the island and we really didn't get a chance to get into any real training. Maybe some guys did. I don't know. I didn't. I was--I was kept busy doing radio work and so really it was--that's all that happened to me really.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Could you image at all when you heard about the atomic bomb, what that was like?

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: I suppose it went through my mind. I couldn't comprehend it though. We--we talked about it, what in the world is that, you know. How--we just couldn't comprehend what an atomic bomb could do. So...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember celebrating on VJ Day?

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. We used to get about--if we were lucky we'd get two cans of warm beer a week, and one of the guys found a case and another--another guy got a fifth of booze from an officer. And, yeah, we did have a celebration. Pretty good one now that you mention it. I had forgotten all about it. But, yeah, we did. We did have a--I was fortunate enough to--you open that warm beer and you lose half of it because it just comes flying out and booze, of course, was not for enlisted then. That was for officers only. So...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So it was probably--well, let's see. What would you say? Was it maybe a couple of years before you finally got home and saw your family?

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah, I got--I got home in mid October of '46 and they--we got off in San Diego. We--and it took a couple of weeks to process us and I got my discharge.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was that reunion with your family like?

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: Oh, it was great. It was great. My mother was worried to death that, you know--in fact, it affected her health really, the fact that I was gone. I was the youngest of the family. In fact, I had three brothers and a sister but I was the only one that was in the service. So my brothers were--the closest one to me was my sister and she was 12 years older than I was. So--but my mother worried about me and I'm sure, I know, it affected her health. So...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But did you have a nice celebration when you got home?

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: Yeah. Oh, yeah. My brothers and all came in. Yeah. Well, we--my mother fixed a big dinner and we had had a party before I left and had a celebration when--when I got home. So, yeah, we--yeah, that was fun to see all the family and they were glad to see me.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any trouble adjusting to civilian life?

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: No, no, none whatsoever. I--that didn't bother me. There for a while I had some flashbacks but it--it dissipated slowly after--after I was home for a while. But, no, I didn't have any trouble.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were the flashbacks to specific incidents on Okinawa?

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: Yeah. That's being--laying in foxholes and thinking you're hearing something that somebody was moving in on you or something and I'd wake up in a cold sweat. It didn't happen too often. Like I say it dissipated after a while and never did--never did bother me that much. But adjustment wise, no, I had no problem whatsoever. I actually had less than two years total, you know. So other guys they had been in several years and on several campaigns and I imagine they might have had a harder time than I did. So...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you think of that experience does one particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: Yeah, the one when I heard that my buddy was killed. That's--that knocked me for a loop. And much more so than when FDR died. But that was--that's the one big thing that hit me the hardest I think, yeah, but that's--that's my story. It's not much I know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Very impressive.

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: It--it was an experience and I'm--I'm glad I was a part of it. In fact, there was several of us quit high school to join the service and I finally made up my credits after in what, 1948. I got married in '48 and went back to night school and made up my credits and got my diploma so--but, yeah, we were--young guys were quitting high school to join the service. And I don't know if that's--that's a fact today or not. I wonder about it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have to get parental permission when you joined the Marines at 17?

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: I was supposed to but I--I--I managed to--I told them I was 18, you know, and nobody bothered to--to look for any identification or anything like that. Okay, if you pass the physical you're--you're on your way. All they wanted were warm bodies, you know. So--but, yeah, I was supposed to have parental permission but I told them I was 18 and they believed me.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was good enough for them?

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: That was good enough for them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You signed your name?

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: Right, right, yeah. So...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Anything else you can think of?

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: Not really. Not really. Like I say I didn't have that much to--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh. It was very interesting. I don't think I've talked to an actual veteran who saw anything on Okinawa. I've talked to guys that were there after it was secured.

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: Oh, okay. Okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I didn't--haven't talked to anyone that was there. I have a family friend that was on Okinawa and I talked to him, called him a couple of weeks ago. I just found out he was on Okinawa.

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: He won't talk.

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: He won't talk.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: He just says I don't want to talk about it.

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: That's understandable, too.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: He's a family friend--all my life friend of my parents.

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: I'll be darn.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And I never knew he was on Okinawa until gee, a month ago. Did you receive any--you probably didn't get a Purple Heart for that punctured eardrum?

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: No, I didn't. No. I probably could have. In fact, I had a corpsman he said--well, I was there at the aid station. He says you want me to write you up for a Purple Heart? I said no, just get me out of here. I didn't get a Purple Heart. I probably could have.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: I wasn't--all I wanted was out, you know. So--but I got two Presidential Unit Citations. Sixth JASCO got one and the Sixth Division as a whole got a--got a unit citation. I have a Combat Action Ribbon somewhere around here but--and then I have a China War Memorial Medal, and that's about it really.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Before I turn off the recorder, anything else? I think we've covered it.

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: Yeah, I think--I think we've covered it. Yeah, yeah, we've covered it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I've done that before when I turned it off and wrapped it up and the guy said wait a minute. Wait a minute, don't say anything.

sp.speaker: Martin Kujala
sp.p: Oh, dear. No, no, I think I've covered it, yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay.
